standard: Each claim is limited to what the cited source actually supports. 'Direct' means preserved fossil, geological or specimen evidence; 'inference' means a conclusion built from multiple lines of evidence; 'debate' means credible published interpretations conflict; 'unknown' means the surviving evidence does not support a reliable conclusion. Access limits are recorded per review; an abstract is not treated as a full paper.

psittacosaurus.scope: Growth, tail integument and the limits of the dietary evidence.
sourcesRead: Erickson & Tumanova 2000: abstract reviewed.
Mayr et al. 2016: abstract, figures and publisher summary reviewed.
Osborn 1923: bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read.

claims.statement: A dorsal row of bristle-like integumentary appendages ran along the tail.
claims.qualification: The structures are preserved as carbonaceous impressions and were imaged with laser-stimulated fluorescence. They occur in bundles, with a pulp cavity that widens toward the base.
claims.context: Specimen SMF R 4970; Early Cretaceous of Liaoning, China.

claims.statement: Long-bone histology supports an S-shaped mass-versus-age growth curve, with maximum growth rates above those of living reptiles and marsupials but below most birds and eutherian mammals.
claims.qualification: The curve is a Developmental Mass Extrapolation model built from a growth series, not a record of individual ages followed through life.
claims.context: Multiple major long bones sampled across juvenile to adult stages.

claims.statement: The tail bristles are probably homologous with filamentous integumentary structures in other dinosaurs, but whether they developed from a follicle is unresolved.
claims.qualification: The authors favour homology with the filaments of Tianyulong and Beipiaosaurus, while noting that a follicle — a developmental hallmark of true feathers — has not been demonstrated.
claims.conflict: Other authors have argued that filamentous covers evolved independently in different dinosaur lineages. The preserved structure alone does not settle the question.

claims.statement: The deep rostral beak and leaf-shaped teeth indicate herbivory, but no gut contents are known for this species.
claims.qualification: Diet is inferred from cranial and dental anatomy. The beak is consistent with cropping, but the plants eaten and the feeding mechanics are not directly preserved.

gaps: No direct gut contents or coprolites.
The function of the tail bristles is not established; display and insulation are both hypotheses.
Body colour and social behaviour are not treated by the cited studies.

maiasaura.scope: Nesting evidence, growth series and the ontogenetic shift in locomotion.
sourcesRead: Horner & Makela 1979: abstract not available; title and later discussion reviewed.
Horner et al. 2000: abstract reviewed.
Dilkes 2001: abstract reviewed.
Horner 1983: bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read.

claims.statement: Nests containing juvenile remains were the basis for the original interpretation of colonial nesting and family structure.
claims.qualification: The nests and juveniles are preserved. Feeding, defence and the extent of parental care are inferred from the association, not observed.
claims.context: Two Medicine Formation, Montana; Upper Cretaceous.

claims.statement: Long-bone histology recognises six growth stages from early nestling to adult, with lines of arrested growth appearing regularly by the subadult stage.
claims.qualification: The stages are histological categories, not exact ages. The study samples multiple bones from an ontogenetic series.

claims.statement: Juveniles walked primarily as bipeds, while adults shifted toward a quadrupedal stance.
claims.qualification: The conclusion comes from morphometrics and beam-theory analysis of limb bones across growth. It is a biomechanical inference, not a trackway record of posture.
claims.context: Ontogenetic series from the Two Medicine Formation.

claims.statement: The dental battery and broad snout indicate a herbivorous diet, but no gut contents are known.
claims.qualification: Diet is inferred from jaw and dental anatomy. The plants eaten are not directly preserved.

gaps: No direct evidence that adults fed or defended nestlings.
The geographic extent and duration of colonial nesting are unresolved.
Body colour, vocalisation and migration are unknown.

coelophysis.scope: The cannibalism reanalysis, juvenile skulls, tooth attachment and the age of the Ghost Ranch assemblage.
sourcesRead: Nesbitt et al. 2006: abstract and open-access article reviewed.
Bugos & McDavid 2024: abstract reviewed.
Fong et al. 2016: abstract reviewed.
Cope 1887: bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read.

claims.statement: The supposed juvenile Coelophysis bones in the body cavity are early crocodylomorph remains; the species is not demonstrated to be cannibalistic.
claims.qualification: The reanalysis examined the anatomy and histology of the material formerly identified as juvenile Coelophysis. It removes the strongest direct support for cannibalism but cannot prove that cannibalism never occurred.
claims.conflict: Older museum displays and popular accounts still describe Coelophysis as cannibalistic. That interpretation rests on the gut contents that this study reidentified.

claims.statement: Two small skulls with large orbits, short flat triangular teeth and thin bones represent skeletally immature individuals.
claims.qualification: The skulls are mostly complete but lack premaxillae and several posterior bones. The differences are interpreted as ontogenetic variation.
claims.context: Ghost Ranch, New Mexico; Rhaetian, Late Triassic.

claims.statement: The teeth were attached by a periodontal complex that includes attachment tissues comparable to those of other early archosaurs.
claims.qualification: Based on histological thin sections of a partial skull. The study documents the tissues, not the bite force or feeding style.

claims.statement: The species is known from the Late Triassic, approximately 215–201 Ma, with the Ghost Ranch quarry generally placed in the Rhaetian and the older Baldwin locality radiometrically dated near 211.9 Ma.
claims.qualification: The numerical range is an occurrence estimate assembled from dated localities, not a direct date on every skeleton. Correlation of the Chinle beds remains debated.

gaps: The age of the Ghost Ranch quarry is still discussed; the archive uses a conservative 215–201 Ma range.
Hunting coordination and social behaviour are not demonstrated by the bonebed.
The full diet is unknown beyond the reidentified gut contents.

borealopelta.scope: Integument, pigmentation, stomach contents and taphonomy of the single known specimen.
sourcesRead: Brown et al. 2017: abstract and open-access PDF reviewed.
Kalyniuk et al. 2023: abstract reviewed.

claims.statement: The holotype preserves continuous fields of epidermal scales and intact horn sheaths capping the body armour in three dimensions.
claims.qualification: This is a single, exceptionally preserved individual. It documents the integument of that animal, not the range of variation in the species.

claims.statement: Melanin is preserved in the organic residues, and the body shows a countershaded pattern with lighter parascapular spines.
claims.qualification: The melanin identification is direct chemical evidence. The reconstruction of the living colour pattern and its camouflage function are inferences from that chemistry and the preserved distribution.

claims.statement: The stomach contents are dominated by fern leaf tissues, with low amounts of gymnosperm material, indicating selective feeding.
claims.qualification: This is one stomach contents sample. It shows what this individual had eaten shortly before death, not the full diet or seasonal range.
claims.context: The 2023 study compares the gut contents with the contemporaneous Gates Formation flora.

claims.statement: The carcass came to rest in a marine setting after floating from a coastal habitat, which explains the exceptional three-dimensional preservation.
claims.qualification: The burial setting is geological evidence. The route from the coastal habitat to the marine site is reconstructed from the carcass's condition and the enclosing sediment.

gaps: Only one individual is known, so individual and population variation are unknown.
The full diet and foraging behaviour are not established.
The ecological function of countershading is a model, not an observation.

kulindadromeus.scope: Integument structure, locality dating and the evolutionary interpretation of filamentous cover.
sourcesRead: Godefroit et al. 2014: abstract reviewed.
Cincotta et al. 2019: abstract and open-access PDF reviewed.

claims.statement: The body bore small scales on the distal hindlimb, larger overlapping scales on the tail, monofilaments on the head and thorax, and branched feather-like structures on the humerus, femur and tibia.
claims.qualification: The structures are preserved as impressions on several partial skeletons. Their colour and full distribution are not known.

claims.statement: The Kulinda locality is Bathonian, approximately 168.3–166.1 Ma, making Kulindadromeus the oldest known dinosaur with feather-like structures.
claims.qualification: The age combines U–Pb dating of detrital zircons and monazites with palynology. It dates the enclosing volcaniclastic deposits, not the dinosaur bones directly.

claims.statement: Feather-like structures may have been widespread across Dinosauria rather than exclusive to theropods.
claims.qualification: The authors argue for a deep origin of feather-like structures. The conclusion depends on homology between filaments in different lineages, which is contested.
claims.conflict: Some authors prefer independent origins for filamentous covers in ornithischians and theropods. The preserved structures alone do not resolve the ancestral condition.

gaps: No gut contents or direct diet evidence.
The function of the filaments is unknown.
Several specimens are partial, and the full body outline is reconstructed.

microraptor.scope: Feather preservation, gliding models and the species-level taxonomy.
sourcesRead: Xu et al. 2003: abstract not available; later descriptions reviewed.
Hone et al. 2010: abstract reviewed.
Chatterjee & Templin 2007: abstract and open-access article reviewed.
Alexander et al. 2010: abstract and open-access article reviewed.

claims.statement: Flight feathers are preserved on both the forelimbs and hindlimbs, and ultraviolet imaging shows that the feathers reached the body rather than drifting away after death.
claims.qualification: The UV study examined the holotype. It establishes the extent of preservation, not the animal's flight performance.

claims.statement: A staggered biplane reconstruction of the hindwings is aerodynamically plausible for gliding.
claims.qualification: The result comes from a planform reconstruction and flight-performance modelling. It does not show that the living animal used this configuration.

claims.statement: Physical models with laterally extended or biplane hindwings were stable gliders, but the tests do not demonstrate the living animal's habitual configuration.
claims.qualification: The models used an anatomically reasonable hip joint with at least 20 degrees of anhedral. Different hindwing configurations performed differently.
claims.conflict: The tetrapteryx and biplane models are both compatible with gliding; the preserved joints and feathers do not uniquely specify one posture.

claims.statement: The distinction between Microraptor gui and M. zhaoianus is not settled.
claims.qualification: The archive keeps M. gui as a named species, following authors who distinguish it. Other analyses treat it as a junior synonym.
claims.conflict: Species-level synonymy changes the count of known microraptorines and the diagnosis used here.

gaps: No direct observation of gliding or powered flight.
The hindwing articulation and preferred flight posture remain debated.
Diet is not treated by the cited flight studies.

mussaurus.scope: The nesting assemblage, growth series and locomotor shift.
sourcesRead: Pol et al. 2021: abstract and open-access article reviewed.
Otero et al. 2019: abstract and open-access article reviewed.
Cerda et al. 2013: abstract reviewed.

claims.statement: The Laguna Colorada assemblage includes more than 100 eggs and 80 individuals ranging from embryos to adults.
claims.qualification: The count comes from a restricted area and stratigraphic interval. It is a minimum sample from the excavated portion, not a census of the whole population.

claims.statement: Individuals cluster by age, which the authors interpret as age segregation within a herd.
claims.qualification: The clusters are preserved associations. Herding and age segregation are behavioural inferences from spatial grouping, not observations of living animals.
claims.context: Early Jurassic, approximately 192.8 Ma; Laguna Colorada Formation, Patagonia.

claims.statement: Hatchlings grew from about 60 g to about 7 kg at one year and more than 1,000 kg as adults, with a shift from quadrupedal hatchlings to bipedal adults.
claims.qualification: The masses and ages are modelled from digital skeletons and growth series. The locomotor shift is inferred from the position of the centre of mass and limb proportions.
claims.context: Hatchling, juvenile (~1 year) and adult (8+ years) individuals.

claims.statement: Juvenile long bones are dominated by fibrolamellar bone with laminar or plexiform vascularisation and no growth marks, indicating rapid early growth.
claims.qualification: Based on thin sections from three juvenile specimens. The absence of growth marks in these juveniles does not mean the species never formed them.

gaps: The nesting site's full extent and the cause of the mortality event are unknown.
Parental care is not directly demonstrated.
The adult growth curve is incomplete.

massospondylus.scope: Growth plasticity, interelemental histology and the limits of the locomotory reconstruction.
sourcesRead: Chapelle et al. 2021: abstract and open-access PDF reviewed.
Chapelle et al. 2022: abstract and open-access article reviewed.
Sues et al. 2004: abstract and open-access PDF reviewed.

claims.statement: Growth was highly plastic, with poor correlation between body size and the number of growth marks across individuals.
claims.qualification: Based on femoral histology from 20 individuals spanning embryo to skeletally mature. The authors infer disparate body masses at given ontogenetic ages.
claims.context: Elliot and Clarens formations, South Africa; Early Jurassic.

claims.statement: Growth trajectories vary between limb bones, complicating a single growth curve for the species.
claims.qualification: The study sampled long bones from 27 specimens. The variation is between elements and between individuals.

claims.statement: There is no histological evidence for differential forelimb versus hindlimb growth rates, weakening a simple ontogenetic postural shift.
claims.qualification: The negative result removes one line of support for a simple shift. It does not prove that posture was constant throughout growth.
claims.conflict: Previous studies suggested an ontogenetic change in posture. The 2022 analysis argues that the histological evidence does not support it.

claims.statement: The skull has a proportionally large orbit and a short antorbital region even in adults.
claims.qualification: Based on four well-preserved skulls, including a juvenile. The description does not establish diet or behaviour.

gaps: Nesting behaviour is known from eggs and embryos, but the cited studies do not establish parental care.
The growth curve and onset of reproductive maturity remain unresolved.

protoceratops.scope: Frill function, appendicular ontogeny and bone histology.
sourcesRead: Knapp et al. 2021: abstract reviewed.
Słowiak et al. 2019: abstract and open-access article reviewed.
Fostowicz-Frelik & Słowiak 2018: abstract and open-access PDF reviewed.

claims.statement: The frill is weakly integrated with the rest of the skull, changes rapidly during ontogeny and has high morphological variance, consistent with a socio-sexual signalling role.
claims.qualification: The study tested four predictions from socio-sexual selection. Three were supported; sexual dimorphism in shape was not.

claims.statement: No sexual dimorphism in skull shape was detected in the sampled Protoceratops andrewsi.
claims.qualification: This is a negative result from a large landmark sample. It does not rule out subtle dimorphism or dimorphism in soft tissue.

claims.statement: Subadult limb anatomy is intermediate between bipedal Psittacosaurus and fully quadrupedal adult Protoceratops.
claims.qualification: The comparison is based on a mostly articulated subadult and a broad sample of neoceratopsians. It documents morphological intermediacy, not a observed change in gait.

claims.statement: Bone histology shows fibrolamellar bone with scarce remodelling and an increase in growth tempo at the subadult stage.
claims.qualification: Based on long bones, frill and rib sections from juvenile, subadult and adult specimens. The growth tempo change is inferred from the femoral sections.

gaps: The frill's signalling function is supported, not proven.
No direct evidence of parental care or herding.
Sexual dimorphism may be present but was not detected in skull shape.

edmontosaurus.scope: Age correction, growth histology and juvenile cranial ontogeny.
sourcesRead: Vanderven et al. 2014: abstract reviewed.
Sharpe et al. 2023: abstract reviewed.
Lambe 1917: bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read.

claims.statement: Edmontosaurus regalis is late Campanian to early Maastrichtian, approximately 73–68 Ma, not the 68–66 Ma range of E. annectens.
claims.qualification: The range is a formation-level occurrence estimate. The Danek Bonebed is upper Campanian; the species may extend into the early Maastrichtian.
claims.context: Horseshoe Canyon Formation, Alberta. The previous dossier age of 68–66 Ma was the range of the younger species E. annectens.

claims.statement: Somatic maturity began at about 10–15 years in the Danek Bonebed sample.
claims.qualification: The age estimate comes from bone histology and growth-mark counts. Even the largest elements lack an external fundamental system, so the exact onset of maturity is modelled.
claims.context: Danek Bonebed, Horseshoe Canyon Formation, Edmonton.

claims.statement: A juvenile skull about 500 mm long confirms that the deep postorbital fossa diagnostic of E. regalis is acquired during growth.
claims.qualification: The specimen is UALVP 60425, a partial skeleton with a partial skull. Its referral to E. regalis rests on a horizontal shelf on the postorbital process of the jugal.

claims.statement: Bonebed accumulation and histology are consistent with overwintering at high latitudes, but do not prove herding or migration.
claims.qualification: The histology compares vascularity with higher-latitude samples. The behavioural interpretation is indirect.

gaps: The soft-tissue head crest is not treated in these claims.
Herding and migration are not directly demonstrated.
The full dietary range is unknown.

miragaia.scope: Neck anatomy, taxonomy and the unresolved function of the elongated neck.
sourcesRead: Mateus et al. 2009: abstract and open-access article reviewed.
Costa & Mateus 2019: abstract and open-access article reviewed.
Sánchez-Fenollosa et al. 2024: abstract reviewed.
Costa et al. 2025: abstract and open-access PDF reviewed.

claims.statement: The neck contains at least 17 cervical vertebrae, eight more than the ancestral ornithischian condition and more than most sauropods.
claims.qualification: The count is based on the articulated holotype. The full neck is not preserved in every referred specimen.

claims.statement: Neck elongation involved cervicalization of anterior dorsal vertebrae and probable lengthening of the centra.
claims.qualification: The anatomical pattern is preserved. The developmental and functional mechanisms behind it are reconstructed from comparison with other stegosaurs.

claims.statement: Miragaia longicollum is treated as a valid species here, but its distinction from Dacentrurus armatus is actively disputed.
claims.qualification: Costa & Mateus (2019) and Costa et al. (2025) argue for distinction based on MG 4863. Sánchez-Fenollosa et al. (2024) propose it as a subjective junior synonym of D. armatus.
claims.conflict: The two positions use overlapping but not identical specimens. The holotype of D. armatus is mostly posterior, while the Miragaia holotype is mostly anterior, so comparable material is limited.

claims.statement: The ecological function of the elongated neck is unresolved.
claims.qualification: High browsing, low browsing, display and sexual selection have all been suggested. The preserved anatomy does not distinguish among them.

gaps: The neck's function is not established.
No direct diet or soft-tissue evidence.

nodosaurus.scope: Specimen provenance, formation correction and the limits of a fragmentary holotype.
sourcesRead: Marsh 1889: bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read.
Lull 1921: bibliographic record reviewed; abstract not available.
Paleobiology Database taxon record: specimen, locality and horizon checked.
Paul 2016: used only for the published size range.

claims.statement: The type and only well-established specimen is YPM 1815, a partial postcranial skeleton from the Frontier Formation at Como Bluff, Wyoming.
claims.qualification: The specimen includes vertebrae, ribs, part of the pelvis, fragmentary forelimbs, a partial hindlimb and osteoderms. The skull is not known.
claims.context: Belle Fourche Member, Frontier Formation; middle Cenomanian, approximately 100–97 Ma. The dossier previously said Mowry Shale, which is incorrect.

claims.statement: The skull is unknown, so cranial anatomy and direct dietary evidence cannot be observed for this species.
claims.qualification: Herbivory is inferred from the animal's relationships and the preserved postcranial anatomy, not from a known skull or gut contents.

claims.statement: The body was covered by keeled osteoderms and low spines, including a sacral armour shield.
claims.qualification: The osteoderms are preserved, but their complete arrangement and the animal's live profile are reconstructed from a partial skeleton.

claims.statement: Length and mass estimates are reconstructions from an incomplete skeleton and comparisons with better-known nodosaurids.
claims.qualification: The figures are published estimates, not measurements of a complete individual. They should be treated as a range.

gaps: The armour arrangement and body proportions are reconstructed.
The formation was corrected from Mowry Shale to Frontier Formation.

velociraptor.scope: Feather evidence and the limits of the hunting interpretation.
sourcesRead: Osborn 1924: bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read.
Turner et al. 2007: abstract reviewed.

claims.statement: Quill knobs on the posterior ulna are direct evidence that the forearm bore large secondary feathers.
claims.qualification: The knobs are preserved on the bone. They establish the presence of feathers, not their colour or full distribution.

claims.statement: Velociraptor was flightless; the forelimb feathers were not used for powered flight.
claims.qualification: The conclusion follows from body size, limb proportions and the flightless anatomy of the animal. The feathers may have had display, insulation or balance functions.

claims.statement: Coordinated pack hunting is not demonstrated by the fossil evidence.
claims.qualification: Associated theropod remains and popular reconstructions have been read as evidence of group hunting. Roach and Brinkman (2007) review the comparative and fossil evidence and argue that coordinated pack hunting is not demonstrated; the null hypothesis is solitary hunting or loose foraging.
claims.conflict: Popular accounts often reconstruct Velociraptor as a coordinated pack hunter; the reviewed fossil evidence does not establish that behaviour.

gaps: No direct evidence of hunting coordination.
The function of the sickle claw is debated.
Body plumage beyond the forearm is inferred from other dromaeosaurs.

anchiornis.scope: Feather arrangement, phylogenetic position and the limits of the flight interpretation.
sourcesRead: Xu et al. 2009: abstract not available; later descriptions reviewed.
Pei et al. 2017: abstract and open-access PDF reviewed.
Wang et al. 2018: abstract reviewed.

claims.statement: The arms, legs and tail bear pennaceous feathers.
claims.qualification: The feathers are preserved as impressions around the skeleton. Their colour pattern is reconstructed from melanosome-like structures in some specimens, not from the impressions alone.

claims.statement: Anchiornis shares derived features with avialans but lacks some deinonychosaur features, complicating its placement.
claims.qualification: The character evidence is preserved; the phylogenetic position depends on the analysis and taxon sample.
claims.conflict: Some analyses place Anchiornis in Anchiornithidae; others recover it as a troodontid. The archive keeps the family assignment provisional.

claims.statement: The aerodynamic function of the wing feathers is not established.
claims.qualification: The feather arrangement is consistent with gliding or display, but no study cited here demonstrates powered flight or a specific locomotor mode.

gaps: Diet is inferred from dentition; no gut contents are treated here.

yi.scope: Membrane-wing anatomy, aerodynamic modelling and the contested function of the wing.
sourcesRead: Xu et al. 2015: abstract not available; holotype description reviewed.
Dececchi et al. 2020: abstract and open-access PDF reviewed.

claims.statement: The holotype preserves a membrane supported by an elongated third manual digit and a rod-like styliform element.
claims.qualification: The membrane and styliform element are preserved in the articulated holotype STM 31-2. The extent of the membrane and its attachment are reconstructed.

claims.statement: Aerodynamic modelling found powered flight highly unlikely and gliding limited for Yi and Ambopteryx.
claims.qualification: The conclusion comes from laser-stimulated fluorescence imaging and aerodynamic calculations. It is a performance model, not a direct observation of behaviour.

claims.statement: The function of the membrane wing remains contested.
claims.qualification: The original authors suggested aerial locomotion. Dececchi et al. found the wing poorly suited to powered flight and limited for gliding, and suggested other wing-based behaviours.
claims.conflict: The preserved membrane is not in dispute; its aerodynamic role is.

gaps: The flight model depends on soft-tissue reconstruction.

sinosauropteryx.scope: Filamentous integument, tail colour reconstruction and post-mortem posture.
sourcesRead: Currie & Chen 2001: abstract reviewed.
Lingham-Soliar 2010: abstract not available; title and later discussion reviewed.
Lingham-Soliar 2015: abstract not available; title and figures reviewed.

claims.statement: The body bears simple filamentous integument, and the tail is the longest known for any theropod.
claims.qualification: The filaments are preserved as impressions. Their homology with avian feathers is debated; they are not branched pennaceous feathers.

claims.statement: The tail preserves pigment-bearing structures interpreted as a colour pattern.
claims.qualification: The structures are preserved; the reconstruction of life colour depends on identifying them as melanosomes and on their distribution. The interpretation has been contested.
claims.conflict: Some authors question whether the preserved structures are original melanosomes rather than decay products or bacteria.

claims.statement: Three stages of post-mortem opisthotonus are preserved in the sample.
claims.qualification: Opisthotonus is a death posture, not behaviour. The three stages document variation in preservational posture.

gaps: The life colour reconstruction is model-dependent.
The function of the filaments is unknown.
Diet is not treated by the cited integument studies.

triceratops.scope: Horn combat, cranial ontogeny and the Torosaurus dispute.
sourcesRead: Farke et al. 2009: abstract and open-access article reviewed.
Horner & Goodwin 2006: abstract and open-access article reviewed.
Longrich & Field 2012: abstract and open-access article reviewed.
Marsh 1889: bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read.

claims.statement: Triceratops has a significantly higher rate of squamosal lesions than Centrosaurus, a pattern consistent with horn use in combat and a protective frill.
claims.qualification: The comparison is statistical. It supports combat as one function of the horns and frill, but does not show how often combat occurred or rule out display.
claims.context: Hell Creek Formation and related Upper Cretaceous deposits.

claims.statement: A growth series from a 38 cm baby skull to about 2 m adult skulls shows four stages of change in the horns, frill and epoccipitals.
claims.qualification: The series is based on ten skulls. The stages are morphological, not exact ages.

claims.statement: Torosaurus is a distinct genus according to Longrich & Field (2012), contrary to the hypothesis that it is the adult form of Triceratops.
claims.qualification: The study coded skulls for maturity and compared frill structures. It found mature individuals of both genera and argued that the ventral depressions of Triceratops are not intermediate toward the fenestrae of Torosaurus.
claims.conflict: The synonymy hypothesis has been defended by other authors using growth-series data. The question is not settled by the available sample.

claims.statement: Triceratops is often reconstructed as solitary, but a juvenile bonebed in Montana and a five-individual mass accumulation in Wyoming show that some individuals were associated. Whether these associations represent a herd, a family group or a time-averaged accumulation is debated.
claims.qualification: The Wyoming bonebed preserves at least five individuals in a single horizon, and the authors argue for rapid burial of associated animals. The deposit does not establish a stable herd, and the Montana juvenile bonebed is a separate accumulation. Older solitary reconstructions and newer group reconstructions are both represented in the literature.
claims.context: Darnell Triceratops Bonebed, Lance Formation, Wyoming; juvenile bonebed, Hell Creek Formation, Montana.
claims.conflict: Some accounts treat the bonebeds as evidence of herding; others emphasize that a mass accumulation can form without a living social group.

gaps: Horn function is supported but not fully resolved.
Herding and parental care are not demonstrated.

tyrannosaurus.scope: Predation traces, growth, feeding and the limits of the soft-tissue evidence.
sourcesRead: DePalma et al. 2013: abstract and open-access article reviewed.
Chin et al. 1998: abstract not available; title and later discussion reviewed.
Carr 2020: abstract and open-access article reviewed.
Cullen et al. 2023: abstract reviewed.
Bell et al. 2017: abstract reviewed.
Rayfield et al. 2001: abstract not available; title reviewed.

claims.statement: A tooth crown embedded in a hadrosaur caudal centrum, surrounded by healed bone, is direct evidence of predation by Tyrannosaurus rex.
claims.qualification: The healed bone shows that the prey survived the injury. The tooth and the prey specimen establish the interaction; they do not establish how often T. rex hunted rather than scavenged.

claims.statement: A large coprolite containing bone fragments is direct evidence of bone consumption, but its attribution to Tyrannosaurus is indirect.
claims.qualification: The coprolite is latest Cretaceous and large enough to be consistent with T. rex, but the animal itself is not preserved. The bone fragments show that a large carnivore consumed bone.

claims.statement: The growth series shows a high growth rate and major changes in skull proportions, including a reduction in tooth count.
claims.qualification: The growth series combines relative maturity, size and histology. The ages and growth curve are modelled, not directly observed.

claims.statement: Theropod teeth, including those of Tyrannosaurus, were probably covered by extraoral tissue when the mouth was closed.
claims.qualification: The inference comes from skull-length-tooth-size regressions, dental histology and comparison with living ziphodont amniotes. It is not a preserved lip.
claims.conflict: Some palaeontologists prefer permanently exposed teeth based on crocodylian comparison and tooth wear. The soft-tissue reconstruction is not settled.

claims.statement: There is no direct evidence of feathers in Tyrannosaurus; skin impressions show a scaly covering.
claims.qualification: The skin impressions document scales on parts of the body. They do not exclude sparse filaments elsewhere. Depictions of a fully feathered T. rex are artistic choices, not fossil observations.
claims.conflict: Filamentous integument is known in smaller tyrannosauroids. Whether large tyrannosaurids retained it is unknown.

gaps: The balance of hunting and scavenging is not quantified.
Social behaviour and parental care are unknown.
The extent of feathers and lips remains debated.
Bite-force estimates depend on the model.

europasaurus.scope: Insular dwarfism, growth series and the limits of the island reconstruction.
sourcesRead: Sander et al. 2006: abstract not available; title and later discussion reviewed.
Carballido & Sander 2013: abstract reviewed.
Carballido et al. 2019: abstract reviewed.
Régent et al. 2024: abstract reviewed.

claims.statement: Bone histology shows reduced growth and adult body size relative to close relatives, interpreted as insular dwarfism.
claims.qualification: The small adult size and growth pattern are directly sampled. The island isolation that drove the dwarfism is inferred from sedimentology and palaeogeography.
claims.context: Süntel Formation, Lower Saxony; Late Jurassic.

claims.statement: The sample includes juvenile and adult material, allowing ontogenetic comparison of the axial and appendicular skeleton.
claims.qualification: The growth series is unusually complete for a sauropod, but not every element is known for every individual.

claims.statement: The phylogenetic position of Europasaurus within Macronaria is unresolved.
claims.qualification: Different analyses recover it as a basal camarasauromorph or among basal brachiosaurids.
claims.conflict: The alternative positions imply different patterns of body-size evolution in Macronaria.

claims.statement: The dentition includes a rhamphotheca-like structure and shows ontogenetic and functional variation.
claims.qualification: The dental morphology is preserved. The soft-tissue rhamphotheca is inferred from the bone surface and comparison with other sauropods.

gaps: The island setting is inferred, not directly observed.

majungasaurus.scope: Cannibalism, feeding traces and forelimb reduction.
sourcesRead: Rogers et al. 2003: abstract reviewed.
Krause et al. 2007: abstract reviewed.
Burch 2017: abstract and open-access PDF reviewed.

claims.statement: Tooth marks matching Majungasaurus tooth size and spacing occur on bones of multiple Majungasaurus individuals.
claims.qualification: The traces are preserved on bone. The trace-maker is identified by tooth size, spacing and serration spacing, and by the absence of another large theropod in the assemblage.

claims.statement: Majungasaurus fed on sauropods and on conspecifics.
claims.qualification: The tooth-marked bones show feeding. They do not establish whether the animals were killed or scavenged.

claims.statement: Whether the marked Majungasaurus individuals were killed by other Majungasaurus or scavenged is unresolved.
claims.qualification: The marks show carcass utilization. Predation and scavenging both produce tooth marks, and the available evidence does not distinguish them.

claims.statement: The forelimbs are short and robust, with reduced muscle lever arms compared with more basal theropods.
claims.qualification: The osteology and reconstructed myology document the reduction. The functional consequence is inferred from lever-arm mechanics.

gaps: The forelimb's function is not established.

carnotaurus.scope: The single skeleton, skin impressions, horn function and formation age.
sourcesRead: Bonaparte 1985: bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read.
Bonaparte 1990: bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read.
Mazzetta et al. 2004: abstract not available; used only for the published size estimate.
Clyde et al. 2021: abstract reviewed.

claims.statement: The only known skeleton preserves extensive impressions of scaly skin.
claims.qualification: The impressions document the skin of one individual. They do not establish colour or the full distribution of scales.
claims.context: La Colonia Formation, Chubut, Argentina; Upper Cretaceous.

claims.statement: The skull bears a pair of frontal horns; their function is unresolved.
claims.qualification: The horns are preserved bone. Display, combat and species recognition are hypotheses, not observations.
claims.context: The horns are above the eyes and are not backed by a frill.

claims.statement: The hindlimbs are long and the tail is deep and muscular; the animal is reconstructed as a fast-running biped, but speed estimates depend on the model.
claims.qualification: Limb proportions support an active predator. Speed cannot be measured from bones alone, and different mass and muscle models give different results.

claims.statement: The La Colonia Formation is approximately 72–66 Ma, but the Carnotaurus specimen itself has not been directly dated.
claims.qualification: The range is the age of the fossil-bearing formation. The specimen's position within that range is not established.
claims.context: The dossier's age is a formation age, not a direct date on the skeleton.

gaps: Horn and forelimb functions are unresolved.
The specimen is not directly dated.

suchomimus.scope: Snout anatomy, forelimb evolution and the fish-eating inference.
sourcesRead: Sereno et al. 1998: abstract reviewed.
Lipkin et al. 2007: bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read.

claims.statement: The snout is extremely elongated and transversely compressed, with conical teeth.
claims.qualification: The skull material is incomplete, but the preserved snout and teeth document the shape. The full tooth count is not known.

claims.statement: The forelimb is robust and bears an enlarged thumb claw; these features evolved before the fish-eating skull adaptations.
claims.qualification: The phylogenetic analysis places the enlarged claw and robust forelimb earlier than the elongated snout. The function of the claw is not established.

claims.statement: A low sail over the hips is formed by blade-shaped neural spines.
claims.qualification: The spines are preserved. Their soft-tissue covering and function are reconstructed.

claims.statement: A fish-focused diet is inferred from the long snout, conical teeth and riverine setting; no stomach contents are known.
claims.qualification: The anatomy is consistent with piscivory, but the animal may have taken other prey. There is no direct evidence that it swam or hunted underwater.
claims.conflict: Some depictions treat Suchomimus as a dedicated swimmer. The dossier does not support that claim.

gaps: The function of the thumb claw is unresolved.
The skeleton is incomplete, so size estimates vary.

deinocheirus.scope: The 2014 anatomy, gut contents and the original description correction.
sourcesRead: Osmólska & Roniewicz 1970: bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read.
Lee et al. 2014: abstract not available; published PDF text and figures reviewed.
Bell et al. 2012: abstract not available; title and later discussion reviewed.

claims.statement: Two partial skeletons recovered in 2006–2009, together with repatriated poached material, made the skull and postcranium known.
claims.qualification: The two specimens are from Bugiin Tsav and Altan Uul. The skull, hand and feet of one individual had been poached and were repatriated in 2014.

claims.statement: The jaws are edentulous and beak-like, and the skull is long and low.
claims.qualification: The skull is known from the repatriated material. The beak's soft-tissue covering is reconstructed.

claims.statement: More than 1,400 gastroliths and fish remains were preserved in the gut, indicating omnivory.
claims.qualification: The gastroliths and fish vertebrae and scales are direct stomach contents from one specimen. They show what that individual had ingested, not the full diet.
claims.context: The gastroliths range from 8 to 87 mm and were found inside the ribs and gastralia.

claims.statement: Tyrannosaur feeding traces on Deinocheirus bones show that it was eaten by Tarbosaurus.
claims.qualification: The traces are bite marks on Deinocheirus remains. They document feeding on the carcass, not the outcome of a hunt.

gaps: The original 1970 description was based on forelimbs only; the old primary reference was corrected.
The function of the hump is unresolved.

tenontosaurus.scope: Growth histology, cranial anatomy and the Deinonychus association.
sourcesRead: Werning 2012: abstract and open-access article reviewed.
Forster 1990: bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read.
Thomas 2015: abstract and open-access PDF reviewed.
Ostrom 1970: bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read.

claims.statement: Long-bone histology shows rapid early growth, sustained rapid growth through subadult ontogeny, and an extended multi-year slow-growth phase before skeletal maturity.
claims.qualification: Based on a large ontogenetic series across a wide geographic range. The growth pattern is reconstructed from bone tissue, not from known ages.

claims.statement: The skull was poorly known before the 2015 description, which clarified its cranial anatomy.
claims.qualification: The description is based on previously collected and poorly preserved material, so some cranial regions remain incomplete.

claims.statement: Tenontosaurus is often associated with Deinonychus remains, but the association does not prove predation.
claims.qualification: The association is direct evidence that Tenontosaurus and Deinonychus remains occur together at some sites. It does not establish predation, coordinated hunting or scavenging; Maxwell and Ostrom (1995) and Roach and Brinkman (2007) treat the behavioural interpretation as unresolved.
claims.conflict: Popular accounts often present the association as a predator-prey scene. The dossier treats that as an inference.

claims.statement: The forelimbs are moderately long and the tail is deep; the animal is reconstructed as facultatively bipedal.
claims.qualification: The postcranial anatomy supports the reconstruction. No trackway or direct observation establishes the preferred gait.

gaps: The Deinonychus association is not a demonstrated kill.
The growth curve is based on histology, not known ages.

argentinosaurus.scope: Holotype, body-mass estimates, stratigraphic setting and the limits of a skull-less giant.
sourcesRead: Bonaparte & Coria 1993: English translation of the original description read.
Mazzetta et al. 2004: abstract and body-mass figures reviewed; full text not read.
Paleobiology Database occurrence record reviewed.

claims.statement: The holotype, MCF-PVPH 1, preserves dorsal and sacral vertebrae, ribs and part of a hindlimb. No skull is known.
claims.qualification: The original description lists three anterior and three posterior dorsal vertebrae, sacral material, a rib and the right tibia. Later work has debated how some limb elements are identified, and an isolated femur has been referred separately.

claims.statement: Body mass was estimated at about 73 tonnes, within a wider range of roughly 60–88 tonnes from different equations.
claims.qualification: This is a regression estimate from limb dimensions, not a measurement of a complete animal. Later studies have produced both lower and higher figures.
claims.context: The estimate depends on restoring missing body volume and on the equations chosen.

claims.statement: The species occurs in the Huincul Formation of Neuquén, dated to the Cenomanian–Turonian.
claims.qualification: The original paper called the unit the Río Limay Formation and gave an Albian–Cenomanian age. The current formation name and age are used here; the fossil itself is not directly dated.
claims.context: Estancia Las Overas, Plaza Huincul area.

claims.statement: Herbivory is inferred from titanosaur anatomy. No skull, gut contents or coprolites are known for this species.
claims.qualification: The absence of a skull means the jaw apparatus and feeding style cannot be examined directly. The plants eaten and the animal’s feeding height remain unknown.

gaps: No direct evidence of diet, nesting or herding.
Body mass depends on reconstructed volume and chosen regression.

camptosaurus.scope: Naming, Morrison Formation context, revised taxonomy and the limits of the feeding evidence.
sourcesRead: Marsh 1879: bibliographic record reviewed; full text not read.
McDonald 2011: abstract and taxonomic conclusions reviewed.
Paleobiology Database and Morrison Formation records reviewed.

claims.statement: Camptosaurus dispar was named by O. C. Marsh in 1879 from Morrison Formation material.
claims.qualification: The name-bearing description is the baseline for the species concept; later referrals and revised diagnoses are separate claims.

claims.statement: McDonald (2011) restricted Camptosaurus dispar and treated several referred species as distinct. The family Camptosauridae is not recovered by every analysis.
claims.qualification: The genus has a long referral history. A specimen labelled Camptosaurus in an older collection is not automatically C. dispar.
claims.conflict: Some analyses place Camptosaurus among basal ankylopollexians without a stable Camptosauridae.

claims.statement: The skull is relatively small, the forelimbs are shorter than the hindlimbs, and the hand bears a small thumb spike.
claims.qualification: These features are preserved in partial skeletons and skulls. The reconstruction as a facultative biped is a functional inference from limb proportions.

claims.statement: The dentition and jaw apparatus indicate herbivory, but no gut contents are known.
claims.qualification: A broad herbivorous diet is well supported for the group; the plants eaten, bite mechanics and feeding height are not directly preserved.

gaps: Social, nesting and parental behaviour unknown.
Many historical referrals need specimen-level reidentification.

dilong.scope: Holotype, preserved integument, contested tyrannosauroid placement and feeding evidence.
sourcesRead: Xu et al. 2004: full text read.
Brusatte & Carr 2016: full text read.
IVPP specimen records reviewed.

claims.statement: The holotype is IVPP V14243, a semi-articulated skeleton with an almost complete skull from the Lujiatun Unit of the Yixian Formation.
claims.qualification: IVPP V14242 and TNP01109 are referred specimens. IVPP V11579 is a referred skull, not the holotype.
claims.context: Lujiatun Unit, Yixian Formation, Liaoning, China.

claims.statement: Filamentous integument is preserved in association with the skeleton.
claims.qualification: The filaments are direct evidence of a body covering. Their colour, density and function are not preserved, and they are not modern contour feathers.

claims.statement: Dilong is a small tyrannosauroid, but its exact position is contested: Brusatte & Carr (2016) recovered it outside Proceratosauridae.
claims.qualification: The archive’s Proceratosauridae label is provisional. Some analyses place Dilong within that family; others place it outside Tyrannosauroidea.

claims.statement: The dentition indicates carnivory, but no gut contents are known.
claims.qualification: Curved, serrated teeth are consistent with a predatory diet. They do not show what prey was taken, whether the animal hunted or scavenged, or how often it fed.

dreadnoughtus.scope: Exceptional appendicular skeleton, specimen completeness, body-mass estimates and missing skull evidence.
sourcesRead: Lacovara et al. 2014: description and specimen list reviewed.
Ullmann & Lacovara 2016: abstract and metadata reviewed.
Voegele et al. 2017, 2020: abstracts and metadata reviewed.

claims.statement: The holotype, MPM-PV 1156, is a partially articulated skeleton preserving much of the appendicular skeleton, pelvis, tail and part of the skull. It is about 45% complete.
claims.qualification: The skull is represented by a maxilla fragment and a tooth. The paratype, MPM-PV 3546, is a smaller partial postcranial skeleton from the same locality.
claims.context: Cerro Fortaleza Formation, Santa Cruz Province, Argentina.

claims.statement: Body mass is estimated from limb bones and reconstructed body volume; published figures vary substantially.
claims.qualification: The original description and later comparative estimates do not agree on a single value. The archive’s 22–38 t range is a set of estimates, not a measurement.

claims.statement: The dorsal vertebrae are extensively pneumatised, and the limb and girdle bones preserve attachment surfaces used to reconstruct musculature.
claims.qualification: Muscle reconstructions are inferences from scars and comparative anatomy, not preserved muscles. The axial skeleton is incomplete.

claims.statement: Herbivory is inferred from titanosaur anatomy; the known skull material is too incomplete to reconstruct the diet directly.
claims.qualification: No gut contents are known. The maxilla fragment and tooth do not establish the plants eaten or the feeding style.

gaps: No direct diet or behaviour evidence.
Mass estimates vary with method and reconstruction.

einiosaurus.scope: Bonebed sample, cranial ornament ontogeny and the limits of the social interpretation.
sourcesRead: Sampson 1995: abstract and bibliographic record reviewed.
Wilson & Scannella 2021: full text read.
MOR specimen records reviewed.

claims.statement: The species is known from two monospecific bonebeds in the Two Medicine Formation, with at least 15 individuals. The holotype is an adult partial skull, MOR 456-8-9-6-1.
claims.qualification: The Canyon Bonebed and Dino Ridge Quarry sample different parts of the skeleton. The association of many individuals is direct; herding is an inference.

claims.statement: The nasal horn is strongly procurved, the supracranial ornament is inflated, and the parietal bears a single pair of elongate P3 processes.
claims.qualification: The ornament is preserved bone. Its function in display, species recognition or combat is not established.

claims.statement: Cranial ornament changes through growth, and the subadult skull MOR 456 8-8-87-1 documents a sequence of ornament development.
claims.qualification: The sequence is reconstructed from a growth series, not from following one individual through life. Size and age are correlated but not identical.

claims.statement: Herbivory is inferred from the dentition and jaw apparatus; no gut contents are known.
claims.qualification: The beak and dental battery are consistent with cropping and processing plants. The plants eaten and the feeding style are not preserved.

gaps: Herding is inferred from bonebed association, not observed.

falcarius.scope: Bonebed sample, transitional therizinosaur anatomy, hindlimb reconstruction and the diet debate.
sourcesRead: Kirkland et al. 2005: abstract and bibliographic record reviewed.
Zanno 2010; Smith et al. 2011, 2023: abstracts and metadata reviewed.
Cedar Mountain Formation records reviewed.

claims.statement: Falcarius is known from a large bonebed in the Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah, including multiple individuals and growth stages.
claims.qualification: The bonebed sample is direct evidence of accumulation. It does not by itself show that the animals lived together or died together.
claims.context: Crystal Geyser quarry, Cedar Mountain Formation, Utah.

claims.statement: The skeleton combines features inherited from carnivorous theropods with modifications associated with therizinosaurs, including changes in the skull, forelimb and hindlimb.
claims.qualification: The transition is reconstructed from anatomy and phylogeny. It is not a direct record of a lineage changing through time.

claims.statement: Hindlimb muscle reconstruction supports a habitual bipedal stance and a relatively short stride for a therizinosaur.
claims.qualification: Muscle attachments constrain the reconstruction, but soft-tissue mass and gait are modelled. Trackways are not known for this species.

claims.statement: Herbivory is inferred from the reduced, leaf-shaped teeth and the wider therizinosaur record; no gut contents are known.
claims.qualification: The dentition is consistent with plant processing, but the jaw mechanism and the plants eaten remain inferences.

gigantspinosaurus.scope: Original abstract, holotype, parascapular spines, redescription and the femoral pathology.
sourcesRead: Ouyang 1992: abstract record reviewed.
Hao et al. 2018 redescription: abstract, figures and diagnosis reviewed.
Maidment & Wei 2006: review record reviewed.

claims.statement: Ouyang (1992) named Gigantspinosaurus sichuanensis on a partial skeleton from the Upper Shaximiao Formation, Sichuan. The holotype is ZDM 0019.
claims.qualification: The original description is a short abstract. The 2018 redescription provides the detailed anatomy and diagnosis used here.
claims.context: Upper Shaximiao Formation, Zigong, Sichuan, China.

claims.statement: The most distinctive feature is a pair of very large parascapular spines, accompanied by relatively small dorsal plates.
claims.qualification: The spines are preserved bone. Their role in display or defence is inferred from their size and position, not observed.

claims.statement: The 2018 redescription recovered Gigantspinosaurus as a stegosaur more derived than Huayangosaurus but less derived than Tuojiangosaurus.
claims.qualification: This is one phylogenetic result. Other analyses differ in the placement of basal stegosaurs, so the family label is navigational.

claims.statement: The femur preserves an osteopathy, interpreted as a healed or chronic abnormality rather than a fatal injury.
claims.qualification: The pathology is preserved bone. Its cause, duration and effect on the animal’s movement are inferences.

gaps: No direct diet or behaviour evidence.

guanlong.scope: Two specimens, cranial crest, Shishugou age and early tyrannosauroid relationships.
sourcesRead: Xu et al. 2006: full text read.
Brusatte & Carr 2016: full text read.
IVPP specimen records reviewed.

claims.statement: Guanlong is known from an adult skeleton, IVPP V14531, and a smaller, nearly complete specimen, IVPP V14532, from the upper Shishugou Formation.
claims.qualification: The adult holotype is partly articulated; the paratype is immature. The two specimens sample different growth stages.

claims.statement: The skull bears a large, thin, pneumatic median crest.
claims.qualification: The crest is preserved bone. A display function is plausible because the structure is delicate, but it is not demonstrated.

claims.statement: The upper Shishugou Formation is Oxfordian, approximately 161–156 Ma.
claims.qualification: The age is based on stratigraphic correlation and radiometric work on the formation, not a direct date on the specimen.

claims.statement: Guanlong is recovered as a proceratosaurid tyrannosauroid in recent analyses, although early tyrannosauroid relationships remain unstable.
claims.qualification: Proceratosauridae is a hypothesis about relationships, not a fixed rank. The composition of the family varies between analyses.

herrerasaurus.scope: Ischigualasto specimens, skull and forelimb anatomy, and the contested position among early dinosaurs.
sourcesRead: Reig 1963: bibliographic record reviewed.
Novas 1994; Sereno & Novas 1994; Sereno 1994: abstracts and metadata reviewed.
Ischigualasto Formation records reviewed.

claims.statement: Herrerasaurus is known from the Ischigualasto Formation of Argentina, dated to the Late Triassic, approximately 231–228 Ma.
claims.qualification: The formation age is radiometrically constrained; the species range is an occurrence estimate, not a direct date on every specimen.

claims.statement: The skull is long and low, with large, curved, serrated teeth and a jaw articulation that permits a wide gape.
claims.qualification: The skull and lower jaws are known from several specimens. Tooth shape is consistent with carnivory; it does not establish prey choice.

claims.statement: The forelimb is relatively short but powerfully built, with a mobile shoulder and a hand capable of grasping.
claims.qualification: The reconstruction of range of motion is a functional inference from joint surfaces, not an observation of use.

claims.statement: Herrerasaurus is one of the earliest branching dinosaurs, but whether it lies inside Theropoda or outside it is contested.
claims.qualification: Different analyses recover it as a herrerasaurid, a basal saurischian or a stem dinosaur. The archive’s family label is navigational.

huayangosaurus.scope: Skull and postcranium, plate arrangement, basal stegosaur relationships and feeding evidence.
sourcesRead: Dong et al. 1982: bibliographic record reviewed.
Sereno & Dong 1992; Maidment et al. 2006: abstracts and metadata reviewed.
Shaximiao Formation records reviewed.

claims.statement: Huayangosaurus has a relatively short snout and a skull that is less derived than those of later stegosaurs.
claims.qualification: The skull is known from multiple specimens. The description supports the anatomy; the evolutionary interpretation depends on the phylogeny used.

claims.statement: The postcranium bears small dorsal plates and at least one pair of tail spines.
claims.qualification: The plates and spines are preserved. Their arrangement and function are reconstructed from the specimen and comparisons with other stegosaurs.

claims.statement: Huayangosaurus is usually placed outside Stegosauridae, as a basal stegosaur.
claims.qualification: This placement is supported by several analyses but is not a universal consensus. Huayangosauridae is used as a navigational family label.

claims.statement: Herbivory is inferred from the skull, jaw and dentition; no gut contents are known.
claims.qualification: The jaws and teeth are consistent with plant cropping. The plants eaten and the feeding posture remain unknown.

hypsilophodon.scope: Wessex material, skull and limb anatomy, the old arboreal hypothesis and track evidence.
sourcesRead: Huxley 1870: bibliographic record reviewed.
Hulke 1873, 1874, 1882: abstracts and metadata reviewed.
Jackson et al. 2010: abstract reviewed.

claims.statement: Hypsilophodon is known from multiple partial skeletons from the Wessex Formation of the Isle of Wight.
claims.qualification: The hypodigm includes skull and postcranial material. The species is small, lightly built and bipedal.
claims.context: Wessex Formation, Isle of Wight, United Kingdom.

claims.statement: The skull is small and lightweight, with a beak and teeth suited to cropping and chewing plants.
claims.qualification: The skull and dentition are preserved. The diet is inferred from anatomy; no gut contents are known.

claims.statement: The old reconstruction of Hypsilophodon as an arboreal animal is not supported by its limb and foot anatomy.
claims.qualification: The arboreal hypothesis was based on an interpretation of the foot and claws. Later anatomical work treated the animal as primarily terrestrial.
claims.context: The disagreement is historical, not a live controversy over the basic posture.

claims.statement: Experimental tracks made by a Hypsilophodon model show how footprint shape changes with sand wetness.
claims.qualification: The experiment constrains how track shape forms; it does not identify a wild trackmaker or reconstruct the animal’s speed.

iguanodon.scope: Bernissart skeletons, thumb spike, integument, posture and the bonebed social inference.
sourcesRead: Boulenger 1881: bibliographic record reviewed.
Verdú et al. 2017; Gasulla et al. 2022; Hooley 1917: abstracts and metadata reviewed.
Bernissart and Wessex records reviewed.

claims.statement: The Bernissart skeletons established much of the modern anatomical concept of Iguanodon bernissartensis.
claims.qualification: The Sainte-Barbe Clays produced many articulated skeletons. They are direct evidence of anatomy; the cause of the accumulation is a separate taphonomic question.

claims.statement: The hand bears a large, conical thumb spike.
claims.qualification: The spike is preserved bone. Its use in defence, feeding or social interaction is inferred, not observed.

claims.statement: Skin impressions show a scaly covering, with no evidence of feathers.
claims.qualification: The impressions sample parts of the body. They do not establish the colour or the full integumentary covering.

claims.statement: Iguanodon was capable of quadrupedal walking, but could also adopt a bipedal stance.
claims.qualification: The posture is reconstructed from limb proportions and joint surfaces. Trackways and the bonebed association are consistent with gregarious behaviour, but herding is not directly observed.

gaps: Herd behaviour inferred from bonebed association.

jobaria.scope: Holotype, revised Middle Jurassic age, vertebral anatomy and the mass-death assemblage.
sourcesRead: Sereno et al. 1999: abstract reviewed.
Rauhut & López-Arbarello 2009: abstract reviewed.
MNN specimen records reviewed.

claims.statement: The holotype, MNN TIG3, is a largely complete skeleton including the skull and most of the postcranium.
claims.qualification: Several individuals, including a juvenile, were found at the same locality. The association is direct; gregarious behaviour is inferred.

claims.statement: The Tiourarén Formation is now interpreted as Middle Jurassic, not Early Cretaceous as in the original description.
claims.qualification: The revision rests on stratigraphic and faunal correlation. The formation has not yielded a single radiometric date that fixes the species’ age.
claims.context: The archive uses a Bathonian–Oxfordian range, approximately 167–161 Ma.

claims.statement: The vertebral column is relatively simple for a sauropod, and the neck is short relative to the body.
claims.qualification: The description is based on the holotype and referred individuals. The functional significance of the short neck is not established.

claims.statement: Herbivory is inferred from the skull and dentition; no gut contents are known.
claims.qualification: The teeth and jaws are consistent with plant feeding. The plants eaten and the feeding height remain unknown.

gaps: Gregarious behaviour inferred from a mass-death assemblage.
Formation age depends on correlation, not direct radiometric dating.

mamenchisaurus.scope: Elongated neck, tail club, uncertain formation age and the limits of the feeding reconstruction.
sourcesRead: Young & Zhao 1972: bibliographic record reviewed.
Xing et al. 2009; Christian et al. 2013: abstracts and metadata reviewed.
Upper Shaximiao Formation records reviewed.

claims.statement: The neck is exceptionally long and is composed of 19 elongated cervical vertebrae.
claims.qualification: The cervical count is based on the holotype. The neck’s range of motion is reconstructed, not observed.

claims.statement: The distal tail bears a bony club formed by fused vertebrae.
claims.qualification: The club is preserved bone. Its use in defence or display is inferred from its shape and from comparison with other sauropods.

claims.statement: The Upper Shaximiao Formation is not reliably radiometrically dated; the archive uses an Oxfordian age of approximately 161–155 Ma.
claims.qualification: Some treatments place the Mamenchisaurus fauna in the Middle Jurassic. The age is a correlation, not a direct date on the specimen.

claims.statement: The dentition indicates herbivory, and the long neck has been interpreted as an adaptation for browsing over a wide area.
claims.qualification: The neck-pose study used Mamenchisaurus youngi, not M. hochuanensis. It constrains plausible poses but does not establish the diet of this species.

gaps: No reliable radiometric date for the formation.
Neck function and feeding height unresolved.

megalosaurus.scope: The first named non-avian dinosaur, the lectotype dentary, Stonesfield context and the limits of a fragmentary taxon.
sourcesRead: Buckland 1824; Mantell 1827: bibliographic records reviewed.
Benson 2008, 2010: abstracts reviewed.
Paleobiology Database specimen record reviewed.

claims.statement: Megalosaurus was named by William Buckland in 1824, making it the first non-avian dinosaur genus to be validly named. Gideon Mantell named the species M. bucklandii in 1827.
claims.qualification: Buckland (1824) described the genus and its material; Mantell (1827) established the binomial M. bucklandii. The 1824 description was based on a collection of bones from several individuals, not a single skeleton.

claims.statement: The lectotype is OUMNH J.13505, a partial right dentary.
claims.qualification: The dentary is diagnostic, but the rest of the historical hypodigm is fragmentary and many referrals are contested.

claims.statement: The Stonesfield material comes from the Taynton Limestone Formation, Bathonian, Middle Jurassic.
claims.qualification: The age is based on the rock unit and its fauna, not a direct date on the lectotype.

claims.statement: The dentition indicates carnivory, but no gut contents are known and the hunting behaviour is not preserved.
claims.qualification: The teeth are curved and serrated. The body-mass estimate of about one tonne is a comparative model, not a measurement.

gaps: No gut contents or behaviour evidence.

minmi.scope: Holotype, paravertebral armour, the Kunbarrasaurus distinction and unresolved ankylosaur relationships.
sourcesRead: Molnar 1980: bibliographic record reviewed.
Molnar & Frey 1987: metadata reviewed.
Leahey et al. 2015: open-access abstract and taxonomic conclusions reviewed.

claims.statement: The holotype, QM F10329, is a partial skeleton from the Bungil Formation of Queensland. It lacks a skull.
claims.qualification: The specimen preserves vertebrae, ribs, part of a hindlimb and armour. The absence of a skull limits cranial and dietary evidence.
claims.context: Bungil Formation, near Roma, Queensland, Australia.

claims.statement: The vertebrae are associated with unusual paravertebral elements, the feature that gives the species its name.
claims.qualification: The elements are preserved bone. Their function in the armour system is reconstructed from position and comparison with other ankylosaurs.

claims.statement: A much more complete skeleton formerly called Minmi sp. from the Allaru Mudstone was named Kunbarrasaurus ieversi in 2015. It is not Minmi paravertebra.
claims.qualification: The distinction is based on cranial anatomy. Older popular accounts that use the Allaru skeleton to describe Minmi are therefore describing a different genus.

claims.statement: Herbivory is inferred from ankylosaur anatomy; the skull of Minmi is unknown, so its feeding apparatus cannot be examined directly.
claims.qualification: The diet is a broad inference for Ankylosauria, not a species-specific observation.

gaps: No gut contents or behaviour evidence.

ouranosaurus.scope: Holotype, elongated neural spines, postcranial variation, locomotion and the unresolved “sail” function.
sourcesRead: Taquet 1976: translated osteology chapter reviewed.
Bertozzo et al. 2017: abstract and specimen record reviewed.
Gônet et al. 2026: abstract reviewed.

claims.statement: Ouranosaurus nigeriensis was named by Philippe Taquet in 1976 from the Elrhaz Formation of Niger.
claims.qualification: The original monograph describes the skull and much of the postcranium. The Elrhaz Formation is Early Cretaceous, Aptian–Albian.

claims.statement: Elongated neural spines run along the back and tail, forming the structure often called a sail.
claims.qualification: The spines are preserved bone. The soft tissue that connected them is not preserved, so the silhouette and function are reconstructions.

claims.statement: The Venice specimen preserves additional postcranial anatomy and shows variation in the skeleton.
claims.qualification: The specimen is referred to the species, but its provenance and completeness differ from the holotype. It is not a complete second skeleton.

claims.statement: Locomotion has been reconstructed as facultatively bipedal or predominantly quadrupedal; the available analyses disagree.
claims.qualification: The debate rests on osteological correlates and body reconstruction, not trackways. The animal’s habitual gait is not directly observed.

gaps: Sail soft tissue and function unknown.

plateosaurus.scope: Large bonebed sample, growth plasticity, body-mass range and feeding biomechanics.
sourcesRead: Meyer 1837: bibliographic record reviewed.
Gunga et al. 2007; Hofmann & Sander 2014; Button et al. 2016: abstracts and metadata reviewed.
Knollenmergel and Frick records reviewed.

claims.statement: Plateosaurus is known from hundreds of individuals, including the Frick and Knollenmergel accumulations in Germany and Switzerland.
claims.qualification: The abundance is direct. Whether the animals congregated in life or were concentrated by drought, flood or mudflow is debated.

claims.statement: Body mass estimates range from about 0.6 tonnes for a 6 m individual to about 4 tonnes for the largest adults.
claims.qualification: The range reflects different specimens, reconstructions and methods. It is not a single species average.

claims.statement: Growth was plastic: juveniles and adults show variable growth-mark spacing, and even isolated neural arches record developmental variation.
claims.qualification: Histology and growth marks sample past growth. The population’s age structure is not known precisely.

claims.statement: The skull and jaw mechanics are consistent with herbivory, but the feeding apparatus differs from that of later sauropods.
claims.qualification: The jaw muscles and bite mechanics are reconstructed. The plants eaten and the possibility of occasional omnivory are not resolved by the preserved anatomy alone.

gaps: Bonebed accumulation and social behaviour debated.
Body mass varies widely with reconstruction.

polacanthus.scope: Holotype, pelvic armour, Wessex context and the unresolved family placement.

claims.statement: The name Polacanthus foxii was first published in 1865 and attributed to Richard Owen; John Whitaker Hulke described the holotype in detail in 1881. The specimen is a partial skeleton from the Wessex Formation of the Isle of Wight.
claims.qualification: The 1865 naming act is an anonymous report of Fox’s lecture; no conventional Owen 1865 description exists. Hulke’s 1881 paper is the first detailed description and the basis for the anatomy used here. The skull is incomplete.
claims.context: Wessex Formation, Isle of Wight, United Kingdom.

claims.statement: A solid shield of fused armour covers the pelvic region, and large spines line the neck and shoulders. The tail lacks a club.
claims.qualification: The armour is preserved. Its defensive function is inferred from structure and position, not observed in action.

claims.statement: Polacanthus is placed in Nodosauridae in broad treatments, but some analyses use Polacanthidae or recover it elsewhere.
claims.qualification: The family label is provisional. The species itself is diagnosed from the armour and postcranium, not from a complete skull.

claims.statement: Herbivory is inferred from ankylosaur anatomy; the incomplete skull limits direct evidence.
claims.qualification: No gut contents are known. The plants eaten and the feeding mechanics remain unknown.

shunosaurus.scope: Abundant skeletons, short neck, tail club and the limits of the behavioural record.

claims.statement: Shunosaurus is known from many partial skeletons from the Lower Shaximiao Formation of Sichuan, including complete skulls and tail clubs.
claims.qualification: The sample is unusually large for a Middle Jurassic sauropod. It supports population-level anatomy but not a complete life history.

claims.statement: The neck is relatively short for a sauropod, and the distal tail bears a small bony club.
claims.qualification: The club is formed by fused vertebrae. Its defensive or display function is inferred from its position and shape.

claims.statement: The skull is known from multiple specimens and has a relatively short snout and leaf-shaped teeth.
claims.qualification: The skull material supports herbivory. The jaw mechanism and the plants eaten are not directly preserved.

claims.statement: Herbivory is inferred from the dentition and jaw apparatus; no gut contents are known.
claims.qualification: The teeth are consistent with cropping vegetation. The diet is a broad inference, not a recorded meal.

therizinosaurus.scope: Holotype claws, missing skull, inferred herbivory and the limits of a fragmentary giant.

claims.statement: The holotype, PIN 551-483, preserves fragmentary postcranial material and isolated manual unguals. No skull is known.
claims.qualification: The manual claws are exceptionally large and curved. Referred forelimb and hindlimb material has been described, but the hypodigm remains incomplete.

claims.statement: Body length is estimated at about 9–10 m and mass at several tonnes, but both figures depend on referred material and reconstruction.
claims.qualification: No complete skeleton is known. The estimates are not measurements of the holotype.

claims.statement: Herbivory is inferred from the wider therizinosaur record, not from the skull or gut contents of Therizinosaurus itself.
claims.qualification: Related therizinosaurs have plant-processing dentitions and, in some cases, gastroliths. Those data support a broad inference but do not record this species’ diet.

claims.statement: No integument is preserved for Therizinosaurus. Feathers are known in other theropods, but there is no direct evidence of a covering for this species.
claims.qualification: The absence of preserved feathers is not evidence that the animal was scaly; it reflects the incompleteness of the material.

gaps: Body proportions depend on referred material.

claims.statement: Turiasaurus is known from a partial skeleton and isolated teeth from the Villar del Arzobispo Formation of Teruel, Spain.
claims.qualification: The skeleton includes a large humerus and other appendicular material. The skull is known from referred material, but the hypodigm is incomplete.
claims.context: Villar del Arzobispo Formation, Teruel, Spain.

claims.statement: The species is one of the largest known European sauropods, with length estimates around 30–37 m and mass around 40–50 t.
claims.qualification: The estimates are reconstructed from limb bones and comparisons, not from a complete skeleton. Different methods produce different values.

claims.statement: The teeth are large and spatulate, consistent with herbivory.
claims.qualification: The large, spatulate tooth crowns are preserved. Herbivory is a functional inference from tooth shape and wear, not a direct observation of diet; the plants eaten and the feeding height are unknown.

claims.statement: A 2024 study proposed that large foraging migrations could help explain the enormous body size of Turiasaurus.
claims.qualification: The hypothesis is based on comparative ecology and growth, not on tracked individuals or direct evidence of migration. It remains untested.

claims.statement: Yutyrannus is known from three nearly complete skeletons: the holotype ZCDM V5000 and the paratypes ZCDM V5001 and ELDM V1001.
claims.qualification: All three preserve filamentous integument. The specimens were purchased from commercial collectors; their exact quarry provenance is not recorded.

claims.statement: Filamentous feathers are preserved on the body and tail of all three individuals.
claims.qualification: The feathers are direct evidence of a covering. Their colour, density and function are not preserved. They are not modern flight feathers.

claims.statement: The largest individual is estimated at about 9 m long and 1.4 tonnes, making it one of the largest known feathered dinosaurs.
claims.qualification: The estimate is based on the skeletons and reconstructed body volume. It is not a measurement of a live animal.

claims.statement: Yutyrannus is a tyrannosauroid, but whether it belongs within Proceratosauridae is contested.
claims.qualification: Brusatte & Carr (2016) recovered it within Proceratosauridae; other analyses place it outside. The family label is provisional.

claims.statement: Acrocanthosaurus atokensis was named by Stovall and Langston in 1950 from the Antlers Formation of Oklahoma. The type is a partial skeleton.
claims.qualification: The original material is incomplete; later referred specimens add skull and postcranial anatomy. The name-bearing specimen remains the baseline for the species concept.

claims.statement: The dorsal vertebrae bear tall neural spines. Their height and cross-section are more consistent with a muscle-and-skin ridge than with a thin sail like that of Spinosaurus, but the soft tissue is not preserved.
claims.qualification: The spines are preserved bone. The soft tissue between them is not preserved; the “ridge” reconstruction is an interpretation of their height and cross-section, not a direct observation.

claims.statement: Forelimb range of motion is consistent with grasping or holding prey, but it does not demonstrate a particular hunting method.
claims.qualification: Joint surfaces constrain plausible movement; muscles, soft tissues and behaviour are reconstructed. No trackway or gut content records the forelimb in use.

claims.statement: The species is known from the Antlers Formation and correlative units in the southern Western Interior. Its Aptian–Albian age is based on stratigraphic correlation, not a direct date on each specimen.
claims.qualification: The geographic range has been extended by referred material, but not every referral is equally secure.
claims.context: Oklahoma, Texas and nearby western North American units.

gaps: No complete skeleton or direct dietary evidence.
Soft tissue of the neural-spine ridge is unknown.

claims.qualification: The original description is part of a broader paper on Cretaceous carnivorous dinosaurs. Later work revised the type series and the family-level diagnosis.

claims.statement: The Dry Island bonebed has produced at least 26 individuals of Albertosaurus. The assemblage is direct evidence of accumulation, not proof that the animals lived as a social group.
claims.qualification: The bonebed is monodominant and includes several growth stages. A flood, drought or predator trap could concentrate animals that did not die together.

claims.statement: Several Albertosaurus specimens preserve palaeopathological lesions, including healed and unhealed damage.
claims.qualification: The lesions are preserved bone. Their cause, effect on the animal and role in mortality are inferences.

gaps: Social behaviour is inferred from a bonebed association.
